review: I've beaten all 3 of the Dawn of War 2 games. They are some of the only RTS games I can enjoy, mostly due to the much lower number of units you are tasked to control. I can actually wrap my head around the tactics, whereas your StarCraft or any other just overwhelms me. The amazing graphics, audio, and dynamic combat with full destruction certainly help things.

Warhammer 40K Dawn of War 2 Chaos Rising is the standalone expansion to Dawn of War 2 and it shows in quite a lot of ways that THQ is not only capable of taking criticism, they can take that criticism and turn it into game fixes and improvements.

Perhaps most notably and most importantly, the single-player campaign. No longer will you be fighting the same battles on the same maps over and over again. Now every single map is a unique entity, properly designed filled with story and gameplay triggers. Although this does mean the campaign is a good deal shorter than in Dawn of War 2 the trade-off is well worth it. Instead of getting only a couple of good missions and a ton of generic ones you now only get good quality missions. This also makes the storyline more condensed as you no longer have 5 generic missions in between every revelation and it keeps your interest up much more efficiently.

The campaign meta-game continues to use the RPG elements from Dawn of War but introduces a new one, corruption. As you play through the game you will find corrupted artifacts and face gameplay choices that result in your heroes slowly turning towards Chaos if you give in to temptation. Although this mechanic is not fully realized, you can't join the forces of chaos, it does give you some interesting choices along the way and a fairly significant storyline consequence towards the end of the game.

Perhaps the most immediate impact of the corrupt mechanic is the various abilities your heroes can unlock as they give in the dark influences. Although many of the abilities feel like just filler a few of them are actually powerful enough that you might opt for corrupting one of your men just to grasp that power. The corrupted weapons work much the same way, some of them being immensely superior to their regular counterparts.

In terms of multi-player the situation is much as the same as in the main game, nothing has really changed except for the addition of a couple of new heroes in Last Stand. GFWL is still present as are the heavy duty matchmaking and connection issues.

Graphically and sound-wise nothing has really changed either, the game still maintains a high quality in both albeit some of that might come from my infatuation with the general art and sound style of the WH40K universe.

When it comes right down to it Chaos Rising is an expansion that improves significantly upon the main game and has taken several steps to correct mistakes made in the original. Although it is an expansion that focuses mostly on the single-player aspects of the game it still manages to feel like a total revival and come out looking superior in every way.

The game perfectly captures the Warhammer 40K atmosphere with intense battles and moral choices that shape your squad’s loyalty. A must-play for fans of the lore and dark storytelling.

We thought the war was over.

We thought the Black Legion had been scattered, the Tyranids broken, the Orks shattered. We thought we had won.

Fools.

Chaos Rising begins where hope ends. The planet Aurelia, long lost to the Warp, returns—and with it, the full, festering stench of treachery, sorcery, and the foulest lies whispered in the hearts of once-loyal men.

You do not play Chaos Rising. You endure it. You bleed through it. You bear it, with grim resolve and your boltgun at the ready.

And if you're strong enough?

You walk out the other side… alone.

🔥 THE CAMPAIGN: HOLY TERROR IN TUNDRA AND WARP
There are no safe missions. No simple supply runs. Every deployment is a reckoning, a crucible of fire and doubt. Heretics rise from the ice, daemons burst from the shadows, and you—Force Commander, sainted hammer of the Emperor’s will—are sent to cleanse them all.

But this time, the rot is not outside your walls. It is within.

The corruption system is no mere mechanic. It is a doctrinal audit of the soul. Choose faith, and you walk the razor path of righteousness. Choose power, and you slide—slowly, inevitably—into damnation.

Each relic of the Warp you equip whispers. Each shortcut tempts. Each time you let a psyker live or ignore a cry for help… the Eye watches.

And one of your brothers? One of them has already fallen.

🧱 COMBAT: CLOSE-QUARTERS CONVICTION
Gone are the factory-halls of base building. Here, your squad is your chapter. Each battle is fought shoulder-to-shoulder with your brothers, knee-deep in blood and broken promises. You flank, suppress, and blast. You charge into daemon-spawned artillery nests with nothing but grenades and unshakeable loyalty.

Micromanagement? No. This is divine choreography.

Tarkus soaks fire like a statue of the Emperor made of ceramite and spite. Thaddeus drops from orbit like an angry angel with a jetpack. Cyrus? The knife in the night, the last whisper your heretic enemies ever hear.

And Avitus? The heavy bolter speaks louder than scripture.

Unless, of course, he's the traitor.

😈 CHAOS: THE ENEMY WITHIN, WITHOUT, AND ALWAYS
Chaos is no longer a faceless threat. It is a voice in your ear, a mocking chuckle when a mission fails. The Black Legion strikes like a poisoned fang—and leaves behind doubt. The daemons don’t just attack—they taunt. The traitor you trusted calls you brother before stabbing you in the back with a warp-infused power blade.

And when the corruption creeps too high?

The ending changes.

You can fall. You can become the very thing you fought. And the worst part? You might like it.

📖 NARRATIVE AND CHOICE: LORE WRITTEN IN BLOOD
This is the most faithful Warhammer game to date—not in graphics, but in tone. You will agonize over decisions. Not for XP. Not for loot. For honor.

There is no perfect run. The Emperor tests all. And Chaos Rising makes you live in the consequences. Brother turns against brother. Innocents die because you didn’t act fast enough. Or worse—because you did.

📜 FINAL CHAPTER EDICT
Dawn of War II: Chaos Rising is not an expansion. It is a trial by fire and frost. A relentless, heresy-soaked march through treachery and tears. It refines everything from the original game—squad mechanics, RPG progression, narrative cohesion—and then sets it all aflame to see what survives.

The ones who endure are not the strongest. They are the most faithful.

Final Judgement: 10/10

A worthy expansion to the original DoW2. I only played the campaign, which is a direct sequel to the vanilla campaign. Chaos Rising campaign has a few differences and additions while the gameplay is mostly the same as the previous entry as a squad-based RTS/RPG hybrid following the same characters. One addition is a new Psyker character who seems to fit in well with the team. Honestly, I did not use him too much since I really liked using most of the other characters instead.  He is like a spell casting character, so he's fun if you like micromanagement. I am lazy and enjoy characters who you can leave AFK and will be just fine, so he's not quite my thing. There are also a few new wargear such as the beloved melta guns.

The campaign is also more streamlined in terms of mission selection. There are a few optional missions still, although they do not repeat, unlike the previous game. So the game is more linear and you cannot prolong the end by doing optional missions forever if that is your thing. All in all the game took about half the time of the original to complete, but it was a great experience and I think has some replayability. 

Chaos RIsing also introduces a morality system. Choices you make in the game, or ignoring squad members desires to participate in certain missions can lead to corruption. An outcome near the end of the game, and even the ending itself are based on this morality system. You can even make new builds through new learned skills based on your corruption or purity. Going in, I thought I would dislike this system since I'm a goody two shoes but it wasn't too bad to stay pure. Now I'm also intrigued to try again with corruption and see what I may have missed.

Characters and story are great as usual. I may even like the story better than the original. If you like Dawn of War 2 campaign, you will definitely want to pick this up to continue it.

I am copying my review from DoW II and update it as Chaos Rising is basically expansion (new missions).

I am really into Warhammer 40'000 lore and I used to play Dawn of War I a lot.
DoW II is completely different game than previous version - it is no longer StarCraft like RTS which I wanted to see, rather some sort of X-COM in real time.
In multiplayer, you don't build and expand base, rather create few squads and battle on the map, hide behind cover, fall back injured etc. 
The biggest issue for me is that you actually can't build any buildings -> just recruit units from the stronghold, some customization options and that's all.
I am missing those big battles from DoW I, assiginig sergants, apothecaries to squad, selecting weapons etc., building defenses etc.
This new model plays great on campaign, it is entertaining and addictive. You can customize heroes with abilities, items, level them up, customize squad etc.
Looking at the current price of this old game, I would definitely encourage everyone to buy and play it.

Comparing to base game
- Singleplayer campaign is still engaging, maybe a little bit too short (15 relatively short missions).
- Higher level cap 30 is way better than 20 (with new abilities and traits) but still, I think there should not be any level cap.
- New abilities, traits, wagers etc.
- Great to fight against Chaos.
- I was playing Chaos Rising running it from DoW II and actually I don't see here any achievements, hours were counted on DoW II game etc.

This part was a lot more action packed and had a more engaging storyline than the first installment. The rest was similar with the game mechanics and the approach to combat. The mission with tanks control was a nice addition.

The pinnacle of squad-based RTS kino 
DaW 2 by itself is fun, but Chaos Rising amps it up; Chaos corruption, new weapons, story etc etc.
Unlike the bombastic world ending story of DaW2, Chaos Rising is a lot more personal as it relates to the Blood Raven chapter and its origins with Chaos, this parallels with the squads relationship with Chaos as the game goes on. 
The true difficulty is how pure do you want to be;
Chaos is a necessary evil, to win you'll need its taint. 
or
Kill all Chaos! All will die by my blade! FOR THE EMPORER!!!

I love how this game gives you hard choices to make. People will die, you will fail and the desire for strength (chaos's temptation) will be ever looming over you.


Pinnacle of Kino, my favorite story telling in all of DaW
10 / 10

Chaos Rising took everything great about Dawn of War II and cranked it up—stronger narrative, tighter missions, and a brilliant corruption system that tested your morality with real consequences. The introduction of the Chaos threat wasn’t just thematic—it reshaped your choices, your gear, and even the fate of your squad. Every decision mattered, and paranoia set in as loyalties blurred.

It’s rare for an expansion to outshine the base game, but Chaos Rising did just that. The atmosphere was heavier, the stakes higher, and the payoff more personal. Watching your veteran squad face corruption and betrayal was both thrilling and gut-wrenching. Easily one of the finest expansions ever made in the RTS-RPG hybrid space.

Actually, I lied. The most regrettable part of this that I cannot excuse and hate with all my soul is this: Occasionally, your units will not respond to any commands. They will not move. They will not attack. They will not even use abilities. The only solution is to get them killed or blow them up yourself. However, if you can't blow up your own units and can't bait enemies towards your now useless squad, good luck! You are now down an entire unit, which can literally determine whether or not you fail the mission, especially if that bugged squad is your designated anti-vehicle unit. I shouldn't have to plan for one of my units going pacifist and deciding to have a picnic in the middle of a war zone while my Force Commander is getting the almighty three shoe beating from Eliphas.

As said, amazing that you can import your progress done so far. The Campaign would be too short otherwise to reach max level, I believe this was intentional and this give a true sense of "sequel" and story progression. You just continue where you left off and the mistery of the traitor until almost the end.

Aside from that, Jonas is literally too overpowered, it can melt down entire armies alone. I bet you could make a challenge on finishing the game entirely with him. Again due to limitations on not being able to max everything out, I would appreciate a reset button to try using more of his powers perhaps with a more support oriented build.

Chaos bar is a nice twist, claws are a joke, additional weapons are quite forgettable expecially if you play immediately after the basic game. You'll probably stick with your favourite guns and care only of better version of them, which appears being also the winning strategy (just keep in inventory a Flame Thrower against Tyranids).

Sad the removal of neutral points that gives incremental benefits that you need to defend, I spent a lot of time in the basic game thinking on how to defend all and pushed me to perform because I needed the extra deployments to make it. It felt very rewarding manage to do it and was very immersive of the neverending war of the 41st millennium.

Chaos Rising is the first expansion for Dawn of War 2 and adds a new faction in Chaos Space marines and a new short single-player campaign. 

This expansion requires base DoW2 to be accessible and basically works as a small add-on on top of the original. 

I mostly played through the campaign here, which actually adds much more to the original's core loop. Not only you get new weapons, the level cap of your squads raised to 30 now and you can get more perks and abilities. You get a new unit, librarian Jonah, who has a bunch of spells and can be effective and melee and range, but has no health, but can very versataile, allowing for both powerful attacking spells, as well as some support and healing, but you have to protect him.
And with addition of chaos, you and your squads can actually be corrupted by the forces of Chaos. Chaos can give powerful abilities and loot, but lead your people into the dark path. If you wish to get rid of the corruption, it is actually a very hard task, since staying pure is a challenge in itself and requires commitment. To get rid of corruption, you have to complete secondary objectives in missions. Sometimes the opportunity for an easier way to remove corruption opens, like donating corrupted gear to librarium or just taking a specific squad member on a mission, but most of the time, staying pure is a big task. Giving into chaos is much easier and faster, but it affects your ending. And some of your corrupted squad members can even betray you later in the campaign.
The corruption really reminded me some Star Wars games, or Bioware RPGs, where you always have to balance your character and make decisions that lead you one way or another.

But the campaign is really short and lacks in side content, there is not much in terms of sidemissions that award you better loot or affecting your corruption, but probably it doesn't need that.

But yeah, it is a good addition. Chaos is a lways fun and an inherent part of W40K. If you play for single-player and campaign, it's good.
